data.text:
Everyone has heard the "FDR knew about Pearl Harbor" conspiracy.

The actual story is weirder than the conspiracy. And it's all in the National Archives.

In 1940, the U.S. quietly cracked PURPLE, Japan's diplomatic cipher. By late 1941, Roosevelt was reading Tokyo's cables to its embassies, sometimes faster than the Japanese ambassador in Washington could. The program was called MAGIC. Fewer than a dozen Americans had access.

On September 24, 1941, Tokyo sent a cable to its Honolulu consulate.

Divide Pearl Harbor into a five-cell grid. Report which U.S. warships are anchored in each cell. Note any moored two-to-a-wharf.

U.S. codebreakers decrypted it within two weeks.

They filed it as routine espionage.

Nobody told Admiral Kimmel.

Meanwhile a junior Japanese diplomat named Takeo Yoshikawa was openly sightseeing around Oahu, riding tour boats past the battleships, sketching, counting masts. The FBI knew he was a spy. They didn't arrest him. Diplomatic immunity.

On November 27, Marshall and Stark sent a "war warning" to every Pacific commander. It said an attack was expected "within days." It named the likely targets: the Philippines. Thailand. Malaya. Borneo.

It did not mention Hawaii.

The night of December 6, the Army intercepted a 14-part Japanese cable breaking off negotiations. FDR read the first 13 parts at 9:30 p.m., turned to Harry Hopkins, and said, "This means war."

He still didn't know where.

The 14th part arrived at dawn on December 7. With it came a separate instruction: deliver the message to Secretary Hull at exactly 1:00 p.m. Washington time. A staff officer noticed something. 1:00 p.m. in D.C. was dawn in Hawaii.

Marshall ordered an immediate alert to every Pacific command.

The Army's radio link to Hawaii was down. Atmospheric interference.

Marshall wouldn't use the scrambler phone. He was afraid Japan was listening on the line.

So the most urgent warning in U.S. military history was handed to Western Union.

Western Union cabled it to RCA's office in Honolulu. RCA's local delivery man, a 22-year-old Japanese-American named Tadao Fuchikami, put the envelope in his satchel and biked it across Oahu.

He arrived at Fort Shafter just before noon.

The attack had ended at 9:45 a.m.

The telegram wasn't even marked priority. Nobody decoded it until the afternoon.

Eight separate investigations have looked at all of this. None of them found Roosevelt had specific advance knowledge. What they found was worse in a quieter way.

The "bomb plot" message gridding Pearl Harbor wasn't forwarded to Hawaii. Yoshikawa's consulate traffic about ship locations wasn't forwarded. MAGIC was held so tightly that the Pacific Fleet commander didn't have access to intelligence about his own fleet. JN-25, the Japanese naval code, wasn't broken yet. We were reading Tokyo's diplomats, not its admirals. The actual strike force orders were invisible to us. The carriers being absent from Pearl Harbor that morning wasn't FDR saving his prizes. Nobody in 1941 yet understood that carriers were the prize. The battleships were the prestige. That's why they were in port.

FDR knew war was coming. He'd been squeezing Japan with oil embargoes and asset freezes for months. He wanted in against Hitler. He expected the first blow to fall in Southeast Asia, not Hawaii.

The truth is uglier than a conspiracy.

A conspiracy implies someone was in control.

We had Japan's mail. We had a Japanese spy openly mapping our anchorage. We had a "this means war" moment fourteen hours before the bombs fell. We had a final alert ready to send at sunrise.

And it got delivered by bicycle.

After the attack was already over.
